_meta.title: Daily-life rules for the Phase 5 population simulation (Xerxes yr 19): how a day is built for each person
_meta.tiers: A attested / B inferred (search extracts capped at B) / C reconstructed. Almost every rule here is C: no source retrieved this session describes an ordinary day at Persepolis. Each row names what it rests on. Values are working values, not claims.
_meta.doc: DECISIONS D-021 (population and day plans), D-023 (guard rota), research/PEOPLE.md P5, research/EVENTS.md

age_structure.note: a stationary population at e0 22-25 (Roman Egypt analogue, SX); the proportions are RECOLLECTION, NOT SEEN (Coale-Demeny West levels 2-4), verify

death_p_year_by_age.note: chosen so the crude death rate with infant deaths lands at E-71's ~40 per 1,000 (C)

birth_p_year_women_15_44.eligible: a married woman (or a woman of a work group with her own household) aged 15-44 whose youngest child is at least a year old; with a child of one, not before the second half of the year
birth_p_year_women_15_44.note: the chance per eligible woman per year, set so the crude birth rate lands at E-70's ~40 per 1,000 once birth spacing removes the women still nursing an infant (C)

infant_death_first_year.note: about half of E-71's 250-350 infant deaths per 1,000 births fall within this (partial) year (C)

marriage.residence: the bride moves to the groom's household (virilocal); a groom who lodges with other workers or in an estate sets up a new house with her in his quarter
marriage.never: a woman with a child, a woman expecting a child, or a man or woman already married
marriage.note: Babylonian marriage agreements (ROTH1987, search extract): women first married at about 14-20, men at about 26-32, and the bride moved to her husband's household with her dowry. B for Babylonia, C for Persepolis. The rate is E-73's 8-10 per 1,000 (no source); no rite is shown (E-73). Q-063

family.note: the children at home are the surviving ones of the mother's own births: first at 16-21 (after marriage at 14-20, ROTH1987), then every 2.5-4.5 years (frequent on-demand nursing spaces births, KONNER1980, an analogy), none after 40; twins in about 1.5 % of maternities; about 43 % of children die before 15 (the E-71 rates, BF1994 analogue); daughters leave at marriage (14-20) and sons stay until they marry (26-32, ROTH1987), so sons up to 29 and daughters up to 19 live at home. All C

mourning_days.note: the household stays home after a death; no source

rise_before_sunrise_h.note: people rise before dawn; a fixed personal tendency, not a daily draw

bed_after_sunset_h.note: lamp oil is costly; a fixed personal tendency

walk_ms.note: walking speed between abstract places (the rendered people walk 1.2-1.4 m/s)

work_day.note: E-60 (PT-WAGE, SX): the gangs work daily 'dawn to mid-afternoon': from sunrise+0.4 h to 15:30 (mid-afternoon is C), with the midday meal at the site. On E-64 heat days (Tmax >= 33 °C in months 3-5) the work stops at noon and the gangs eat and go home (C; Q-062). The Phase 3 slice's sunset-0.6 h end is withdrawn

heat_rest.note: E-64 midday rest in the heat (the rule is C; Tmax 36-38 C in Jun-Aug is A)

winter_half_gangs.note: E-62 'gang strength x 0.5' (C, Q-037): here each ten works every other day, the others stay in the town

evening.note: chances per evening of the real options open to a household (brief 9.5: people visit, trade, idle); weather and daylight change them; relationships weight whom they visit

exchange_in_kind.note: barter of ration goods between households (grain, beer, a jar, a tool) at the quarter's open space; no market with coins (blocklist coins-everyday; Q-011)

winnowing.note: grain is winnowed by tossing it into a wind that carries the chaff off; in still air the threshed heap waits and the straw is turned (a working wind of about 2 m/s is C); the weather's hourly wind decides the morning's and the afternoon's work on the floor (E-43, Q-140)

household_bread.durations_note: kneading and baking take longer the more there are to feed, and vary with the woman and the day's fire (about 0.25-0.55 h and 0.5-1.0 h for five to eight eaters); the time between the bread and the meal varies (C)
household_bread.note: saddle-quern grinding at home (quern type B) for everyone who eats in the house, shared among its women (about 0.3 h per eater a day: ethnographic accounts give 2-3 h a day for a family of five to six, NOT SEEN, C); flat bread baked every other day (C)

meals.note: house_habit_h: without clocks each house judges midday and evening by its own shadow marks and chores, so its midday meal and supper keep their own time within ±0.25 h of the others (a fixed habit of the house, the same every day; C). Three meals: bread before work (in hand if one leaves before the household eats), a midday meal at work or at home, and the evening meal with the household, which is the main one and is eaten together. Daily bread issues to workers exist (IR-PET, B) and rations were grain, flour, beer and wine (A/B); the number and times of ordinary people's meals are not recorded. Herodotus (1.133, a Greek claim) says Persians ate little solid food and many courses of dessert. Durations follow the causes listed (household size, a baking day, winter evenings, a birthday); all C (Q-064)

night_gap_max_h.note: the longest gap between a baby's feeds at night, by its age (each row: up to that age in months, the hours): 3.5 h under two months, 4.5 h to six months, 6 h to a year. Night feeds are counted by night_feeds; this bounds how they are spaced (S4 of shadow review r7: 4 h 51 min unfed at night at 0 months). The !Kung analogy (KONNER1980) has babies sleeping at the breast and nursing through the night; the hours are a modern paediatric rule of thumb (newborns fed every 2-3 h round the clock, longer night stretches from about 3-6 months: RECOLLECTION, NOT SEEN, verify). C (Q-339)

infant_care.note: infants are nursed on demand, by day and by night, wherever the mother is (the !Kung analogy: bouts every few minutes; here one feed every 1.6-2.8 h stands for them), carried on her back when she works or walks, in her lap when she sits, and asleep beside her at night; children of one to two years are still nursed a few times a day. Twins: one on the back, one at the front. All C (Q-061)

sleep.note: babies of 0-3 months sleep about 14-17 h in 24 and of 4-11 months 12-15 h, mostly in short naps (the National Sleep Foundation's recommendations, Hirshkowitz et al. 2015, Sleep Health 1: modern infants; RECOLLECTION, NOT SEEN, verify). Here a baby under four months is awake from each feed for a short while (each row: up to that age in days, the least and the most hours awake after a feed: 0.5-0.9 h under a month, rising with age) and asleep until the next feed, wherever the mother is: on her back while she works or walks, in her lap, on a mat beside her; when the feeds come close together it is awake no longer than the row's most + awake_max_extra_h from its last waking and falls asleep at the breast; from four months three naps (the first in hours after the mother wakes, the others in clock hours) and asleep from about sunset + 0.6 h, before the mother goes to bed. All C. Was: asleep only when the mother slept or at three fixed naps, so a baby of two months was awake 5.5 h at a stretch and asleep 11 h in 24 (shadow review r4, S5)

water_trips.note: wells and river-fed canals only (no qanats: Q-052); women and children fetch water (C)

guard_rota.break_note: each man at a post is relieved once in his watch for bread and water at the hearth by one of the patrol pair, who stands in; the patrol man eats between his fourth and fifth stand-in, the second four breaks coming break_mid_gap_h later to leave him the time (C, Q-060; the reviewer notes that shorter watches were the usual ancient practice: not modelled)
guard_rota.note: decimal files of ten (HDT 7.81, a claim about the army: B); three watches (Phase 3, C); a five-day forward rotation A-B-C-off-off so every man stands one watch in five days' three and has two days off (C). Posts rotate by three places each cycle; the patrol pair covers a sick man's post, then a man is called from an off file

guard_family_share.note: population.json: 200 garrison family members in the town (C); about 60 of 100 guards have a wife and children there

guard_off_day.drill_note: practice with the bow and the spear at the practice ground below the Terrace: XEN-CYR 1.2.9-12 has the young Persians who keep guard round the public buildings by night practise shooting and the javelin by day (a Greek claim, B; RECOLLECTION, NOT SEEN, verify); the rate C. water_duty, town_errand, drill and river are each a day's draw, done once in the off-watch hours when the light and the weather allow (S2 of shadow review r6: water_duty and town_errand were read by no code; D-186)
guard_off_day.ration_carry: the garrison's monthly ration is carried up from the Terrace depot by off-duty men
guard_off_day.note: brief 9.1: guards guard, escort, check authorisations, eat, sleep, gamble and idle; family visits and fatigue duties are C

treasury_doubling_guards.note: E-81 while silver is weighed out (E-05) or a courier's letter reaches the Treasury (E-20)

camp_women_needed.rule: bread for the gang: all women on full days; in the winter months half of them on alternate days; mothers of infants under one year stay home
camp_women_needed.tasks_note: flour: the camp's grain and flour as goods: sacks of barley carried up from the camp's grain at the depot (the stair foot) to the querns, and the flour ground there carried to the ovens; in the detailed tier every carried sack is taken from one stock and added to another, grinding turns the querns' barley into flour (grind_h_per_sack) and the bakers' kneading draws on the ovens' flour (knead_sacks). Was: sacks of flour from the depot set down at the querns (S6 of shadow review r5; C)
camp_women_needed.grind_note: a sack of 3 BAR of barley (about 29 l, 19 kg) takes a woman about 18 h at a saddle quern (about 1 kg of flour an hour: experimental grinding, RECOLLECTION, NOT SEEN, verify; C)
camp_women_needed.camp_grain_note: each morning the storehouse sends up the camp's barley to the depot when it holds fewer than 12 sacks (C; the gang's bread is mostly from the town mill's flour, E-07, which the detailed slice does not carry)
camp_women_needed.note: the work-camp women's group (C) serving the Terrace gangs

messenger_duty.rule: a letter for the Treasury goes up with the first messenger on duty; other letters to the official building or the storehouse; messengers alternate days at the station
messenger_duty.note: the relay (HDT 8.98, B claim); the station's own messengers and their rota are C

official_round.rule: calendar-driven: payments -> the Treasury; deliveries -> the storehouse; couriers -> letters at the official building; construction -> the building site; otherwise the official building
official_round.note: PT letters: 'Budkama declares' (an official orders a payment, SX); rounds C

dispute_context.rule: the queue on an issue day, the work place, the well, or the canal in low-water months
dispute_context.note: E-74 rates x3 on short rations (CE-03), x1.5 when the river is low (CE-19)

harvest_draft.note: population.json town derivation: 'harvest labour sent to fields in summer (5-15 %)'; kurtas of the state groups (not the skilled stonecutters or the Terrace porters) are sent to reap on the state fields on about 8 % of days in the harvest months (C)

job_tasks.note: the real alternatives inside each job, drawn per person and day (weights C). Each is a different place or activity the job involved; none is a timing shift. Where the calendar drives a task (issues, deliveries, milling, couriers, slaughter, drum arrivals) the calendar decides, not chance.

treasury_workshop.note: treasury personnel were handlers of wood, carpentry supplies, precious metals and textiles, storekeepers, supervisors and recorders (HENK2023, B): they moved goods between the stores, the workshops and the Treasury as well as working them; outwork at home and the group's own grinding are C

treasury_staff.note: inside the Treasury, each half-day one of a staff member's own tasks by trade: treasury staff were handlers of precious metals, storekeepers, supervisors and recorders (HENK2023, B); shining the metal, weighing and recording the weights, keeping the store (its seals), stacking what the porters carry up, recording what came in and went out, carrying between the store and the halls (weights C). The hides of a slaughter (E-12, CE-07) are received by two storekeepers, E-12's 'two hide receivers', at the carriers' own hour and for as long as counting and recording them takes (Population.hideDelivery). Was: a 'receive' draw of 0.15 per half-day on any day on or after a slaughter (S1 of shadow review r6)

terrace_porter.note: population.json 'porters, water carriers, deliveries' (w 40): goods up to the Treasury store, barley up to the work camp's querns (was flour: S6 of shadow review r5), water jars to the building site, waiting at the depot

weaver.note: women's work groups in textile work (C); spinning at home, washing and dyeing wool at the water and delivering cloth to the treasury store are C

miller.note: grain to the mill and flour back to the stores (PF 28-33, A for the flow); who carried it is C

groom.note: relay horses (HDT 8.98, B claim) and stable horses on grain rations (POTTS2023, B): tending, watering at the river, cleaning the stalls, leading horses along the road

craftsman.note: Persepolis West Area B: kiln, bone pits and pigment making incl. Egyptian blue whose palette matches the Terrace (B); clay from the river and delivery to the Terrace are C

caretaker.note: population.json 'palace caretakers, cleaners, lamp keepers (palaces shut while the court is away)' (C)

shepherd.note: the state flock is grazed on rotating grounds (C)

labour_gang.note: hauling drums up the ramp to the column now rising, building up the earth ramp, carrying water for mortar, unloading drums from the quarry at the yard (on arrival days)

brick_squad.note: at the hall walls a brick squad shares out the work, morning and afternoon drawn separately: laying, carrying dried bricks from the stacks to the wall, mixing mud mortar and carrying its water; in the brick-mould months (2-5, E-63) the squads alternate between the brickyard and the walls

scribe.note: Treasury scribes record payments and issues and seal receipts that go back as records (IR-PET, B); counting in the store, taking tablets to the official building and sealing letters are C

gardener.note: research/SETTLEMENT.md §4: partetaš workers tending royal gardens (B); Pasargadae beds divided by channels (B, analogy); figs to the stores (CDLI-PF, E-46 -> E-10). The gardens' work, one choice for the morning and one for the afternoon: hoeing, weeding and sowing the beds; opening and closing the runnels between the beds; pruning (winter) or tending the trees, picking in the fig months (E-46); carrying produce to the store (E-10); carrying dung from the stockyard; clearing silt from the garden channel. The tasks are attested in kind for Achaemenid gardens only by the partetaš workers; the seasonal weights are C

work.trade_note: a son of 12-13 in a craftsman's, a scribe's, a gardener's or a storekeeper's house of the town goes with his father to his work on one day in two and learns it beside him (C; S6 of reviewer B, r5)
work.note: hours of work a day by age (5-6, 7-9, 10-11, 12-13): girls mind the little ones (the eldest girl is the house's child-minder while the mother is out), fetch water, grind beside the mother (from 10; from 12 their share of the household's grinding with the women), spin, gather dung and brushwood and shape dung cakes, help at the oven, carry the midday bread out to the men; boys herd the household's animals on the stubble and fallow (plain), fetch water and fuel, run errands with loads, scare birds from the ripening crop before the harvest, and from 10 go out with the men to the ploughing and sowing. Village time-use studies find children's work rising with age to near-adult days in the early teens (Nag, White and Peet 1978, a Javanese and a Nepali village: NOT SEEN beyond the abstract); the hours here are C (Q-143)

bed_after_sunset_h.note: children go to bed earlier than adults (C)

children.minded_note: a child under eight is not left alone at home: when no other grown-up of the house (a grandparent, an older daughter, a co-wife) stays at home through the mother's working hours away, the child goes with her to the field, the workshop or the work camp and plays near her (C, Q-061)

persian_boys_training.who: boys of households of standing only: an official's, a steward's, a scribe's, a priest's, a storekeeper's or a Persian guard's (XEN-CYR 1.2.15: only those who can maintain their children without work send them; HDT 1.136 generalises to all Persians; Q-146, D-138)

children.note: children go with their mothers to the queue, to kin and to the harvest; Persian boys from five 'are taught to ride, to shoot with the bow and to speak the truth' (HDT 1.136, a Greek claim, B); the rest is play and errands (C; Q-065)
children.chores_note: from about seven, children fetch water, mind the younger ones, gather dung and brushwood for the fire, grind with the women (girls) and run errands, morning and afternoon (C)

homemaker.note: a woman's day: the quern and the bread (household_bread), water, the ration queue, visits, exchange in kind, washing at the water, spinning and weaving, the children; in the plain the harvest, threshing and fruit picking take the whole household on most days (E-41 ... E-46), and the late afternoon goes to grinding, spinning, sheaves to the threshing floor or the lane (C)

children_under_five.outing_from_3_note: from three a child is out of doors with the other children most of the day in fine weather (C, D-082)
children_under_five.minder_note: the house's child-minder (the eldest girl of 7-13, else a boy of 8-13) has the little ones of one to four through the mother's working absences of 1.5 h or more, and in one of the mother's spells of work at home in two (up to 1.5 h each, at most three a day), so that she works unhindered; she may take them out to the lane for a while. Planned from the little one's side, both plans from one schedule (Population.mindDay; S2 of shadow review r5; C)
children_under_five.note: infants: see infant_care (nursed on demand by day and night, on the mother's back only while she works or walks); toddlers play near her and nap at midday. While she works away for hours a toddler goes along or is left with a grandparent or a kinswoman and is wherever that person's own day takes them; on some days the small ones are taken outside the door, or to a neighbour's or kinswoman's house in the same lane (not in rain or dust); an older brother or sister takes them along to play (C)

elders.note: old people sit in the lane, visit kin, do light work (grinding and spinning; mending), mind the children, run small errands, rest, and nap in the afternoon; in the plain an old man sits out by the household's crop or the threshing floor (more at the harvest) and old people see to the animals. Mornings and afternoons are each several of these in turn (C)

men_of_standing.note: a man of standing (an official, a steward, a priest, a scribe, a storekeeper) has no mending of tools and baskets in his hours at home: the servants and the labourers do that; his go to the household's affairs (with the servants where there are any), a caller at the house, a scribe's or storekeeper's own accounts on a tablet (S7 of shadow review r5; C)

women_winter.note: in the winter months (9-11) a woman's hours at home go to the spindle and the loom: the fields are quiet, the days short and cold, and the wool of the spring shearing (E-47) and the year's cloth are worked indoors (C; a village practice, no Achaemenid source). From noon on, a woman at home who has not yet had the spindle or the loom in her hands for spin_min_h today takes it up before anything else (C), so no winter day at home passes in talk and rest. Was: the same weights all year, so a winter day at home was 7 h of rest and 25 min of spinning (shadow review r4, S7)

women_day_off.note: a woman's day at home off her work (a camp woman's winter half day, a weaver's day at home): the spinning the household needs fills it before rest (C, S7)

women_rest_cap_h.note: a woman's rest at home in daylight: beyond this her hours at home go to the spindle, the quern, the lane and the household (the E-64 sleep in the heat is not counted); a mother minding small children is at work while she minds them, but the spindle goes on in her hands (C, S7)

men_rest_cap_h.note: an able farming man's rest at home in daylight on a day of work: beyond this he sees to the animals, mends the tools, does the season's jobs about the house or talks with the household (the E-64 sleep in the heat is not counted). Winter keeps its longer rest ('little field work in winter': PEOPLE.md P5.6 winter 0.15, E-62). C (shadow review r4, S1)

farm_chores.note: the season's jobs of a farming man in his hours at home (C): the sickles and baskets before the barley harvest (E-41), the winnowing gear while the floor is in use (E-43), the plough and yoke before and during the ploughing (E-40), the roof before the first rains (CE-20), the ewes at lambing (E-48), the animals stall-fed on the stored straw in winter; otherwise mending tools and baskets

list.why: sharpening the sickles and mending the baskets and ropes for the harvest
mending the winnowing forks, the sieves and the sacks
plastering the roof with mud and straw before the rains
mending the plough and the yoke for the ploughing
with the ewes and the new lambs
feeding the animals the stored straw

home_hours.note: the hours at home between tasks: men rest, mend tools and baskets, see to the household's animals (plain: population.json farming_household animals, C) and talk with the household; women rest, grind, spin and talk, or sit outside the door in the lane with the other women, spinning and talking, the small children about them (not in rain or dust); both sleep through the heat of the day in the E-64 months (C)

floor.why: readying the threshing floor for the harvest: clearing it, levelling it and beating the ground hard
floor.note: the floor must be ready before the sheaves come (E-43 follows E-41/E-42); only in the 12 days before the barley harvest opens (E-41 day_window)

vines.tool: a pruning knife and a hoe

why.11: pruning the vines before the buds break
why.12: pruning the vines and tying up the canes
why.1: hoeing round the vines and tying up the new shoots
why.2: hoeing round the vines and tying up the new shoots
why.other: tending the vines and their water channels

vines.note: vines and wine are PF commodities (IR-FOODAG, B); the plain's vines leaf out in April and are picked in Sep-Oct (research/PLAIN.md §3, C); pruning before the buds break and hoeing in spring are C

trees.tool: a pruning knife and a hoe

why.12: pruning the fruit trees and clearing their water channels
why.other: tending the fruit trees and their water channels

trees.note: figs, apples, pears, pomegranates and mulberries are PF commodities (IR-FOODAG, B); orchards in a ring round each village (plain.json orchards_gardens, C)

why.6: digging over the garden beds by the village and manuring them
why.7: digging over the garden beds by the village and manuring them
why.8: digging over the garden beds by the village and manuring them
why.other: hoeing and weeding the garden beds by the village and letting in the water

garden.note: orchards and gardens in a ring round each village (plain.json orchards_gardens, C)

fodder.tool: a sickle and a carrying cloth
fodder.why: cutting green fodder for the animals along the canal banks and the field edges
fodder.note: a farm's draught animals, sheep and goats (population.json farming_household, C) are fed green fodder while it grows (C)

straw.why: carrying the threshed straw home from the floor for the animals' winter fodder
straw.note: after the threshing (E-43) the straw is stored for the winter (C)

sesame.why: cutting the sesame sown in the spring and standing it in bundles to dry
sesame.note: sesame is attested (PF 56, A); sown in the spring (E-44) and cut in September (research/PLAIN.md §3, C)

fuel.tool: a rope and a carrying cloth
fuel.why: gathering brushwood and dung for the winter's fires
fuel.note: dung and brushwood are the household's fuel (lives.json children.work, C); stocked before the cold

market.why: exchanging produce in kind in the lanes of the town: barley for oil, a jar or cloth
market.note: exchange in kind, no coins (lives.json exchange_in_kind; blocklist coins-everyday); the village lane when the town is more than 1.5 h away

farm_men_other_work.note: a farming man's day when the calendar's rows (E-40 ... E-50, the water turn) and the field draw (population.json field_fraction_by_sex) give the household no task: the season's other work, drawn by weight for the month (C). Outside winter every such day has work (Q-057 lists no cause for a day without it); in the winter months 9-11 'home' keeps the day at home ('little field work in winter': PEOPLE.md P5.6 winter 0.15, E-62), with the winter jobs of home_hours.farm_chores. Each option names the row it rests on. Was: a day at home mostly at rest (shadow review r4, S1, Q-220)

herders.band: herding families in their tents: each tent a man and his wife with their surviving children (lives.json family), now and then an old parent or, in a young man's tent (34 or under), an unmarried younger brother; the band has E-49's 5-40 people; the eldest tent's man leads it
herders.note: E-49 cites the Qashqai as its analogue (SX: north in April, south in September), and the Qashqai migrate as families; HDT 1.125 (FT, a Greek claim, B) names the Dai, Mardi, Dropici and Sagartii among the Persians as 'all wandering herdsmen'; E-49's participant row lists herders, dogs and donkeys. Decided (D-150): a band is herding families, the make-up its cited analogue shows, not a drive crew (the state's drives of the king's sheep to Susa are E-13, shepherds only). The day (all C): the women milk the ewes and goats before dawn and after the flock comes in, in the months after the lambing (E-48: lambs in months 10-12, milk into early summer; none in the autumn passage), make the curds and bake, strike and pitch the tents and load the donkeys; the flock moves ahead with the men and the older boys and the dogs, grazing as it goes, and lies up through the midday heat (a halt of about an hour on a cool day to three and a half at 32 C or more); the families follow with the loaded donkeys, one man in four with them by turns, and reach the new camp first; on about one day in four the band stays where it is; two men of the band watch the flock with the dogs through the night by turns (the first until about one in the morning, the second until the camp wakes) and walk with the donkeys the next day, sleeping at the halt and in the afternoon. The Basseri of Fars, whose migration crosses the Marvdasht plain, are described in this way (F. Barth, Nomads of South Persia, 1961: RECOLLECTION, NOT SEEN, verify). Was: one plan for the whole band to the minute, asleep at sunset, nobody with the flock (shadow review r4, S4)

travellers_stay.note: a party staying at the road station (E-21): the evening after the meal by the fire with the party, at knucklebones or in the lanes of the lower town until their bedtime (evening); each day's business in turn (the leader: the official building, the storehouse, the Treasury's scribes; the others: the animals and gear, trading in kind, the lanes, waiting at the stores), then the rest of the morning and the afternoon each: rest (a sleep in the heat), mending harness and gear, watering the animals at the river, knucklebones, or the lanes (C)

affinity.note: how relationships change: disputes sour them, visits and shared grief warm them, everything drifts back to its base over about a month (brief 9.5)

familiarity.note: memory of the player (brief 9.5): a guard who stopped you yesterday recognises you today; a baker you watched nods; it fades over a week or two
